Isn't that some intellectual property thing? Or can you not copyright a website interface? I was always confused how reddit was able to copy digg so much and now voat as well. I was showered with downvotes whenever I asked reddit, so hopefully I'll get a real answer finally.
How is it that places like voat and reddit can use the same basic interface as digg and get away with it?

It's probably different enough that it's okay. Or just not patented.

Nintendo has the intellectual rights or patents or whatever on the d-pad as well, other companies get around it by just designing it slightly differently, even if the functionality is the same.
Voat uses some of reddit's CSS, but that is OK because of the license that that CSS is under. None of them have ever patented it, so they can use it.

I've spoken to some lawyers about this general issue and I may be butchering their advice, but my cliff notes would be that software patent/copyright laws are incredibly complex, but ultimately can not protect against high level clones. For instance there are about a million Minecraft clones with near identical functionality but you can't really protect the vague idea of a game built around the manipulation and crafting of large voxels.

It's not clear to me exactly how sites like Amazon got away with things like patenting "one click checkout" or Apple patenting "slide unlock", but I assume the difference there is that it's on a micro scale as opposed to a macro scale.

My understanding of patents is that you can't get one on a design that's simple enough for anyone experienced in the field can come up with, which is why Apple and Samsung are fighting over whether or not the patent was valid on the slate smartphone. I imagine the same can be said for interfaces.
Digg ripped off Slashdot and Kuro5hin, if you want to get technical.

The basic premise that has been used for much of the innovation that has occurred in the last century or so is that you can patent the design of something but not the overall functionality. Meaning that, like transmission designs in the early 20th century and the design of the stick shift and the steering wheel, you can patent your take on it but not the overall functionality of it ( a circle that steers a car isn't patentable, but one that uses velvet with a unique pattern can be).

This has been trampled on in recent cases involving tech UI and functionality, but in each case there has been, in some cases, successful appeals that overturned these decisions.

Let's hope this holds true!
